title: Prior Knowledge - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Explore the role of Prior Knowledge and standard practice when establishing technological uncertainty in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: In Canada's federal SR&ED program, prior knowledge is the existing scientific or technological knowledge base—a claimant's internal resources plus publicly available knowledge at the start of a project. For businesses claiming SR&ED tax incentives, work qualifies only where gaps in that knowledge create scientific or technological uncertainty; merely acquiring existing knowledge or know-how is ineligible.

body.text: In Canada's federal SR&ED program, prior knowledge is the existing scientific or technological knowledge base—a claimant's internal resources plus publicly available knowledge at the start of a project. For businesses claiming SR&ED tax incentives, work qualifies only where gaps in that knowledge create scientific or technological uncertainty; merely acquiring existing knowledge or know-how is ineligible.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is the federal government's largest single source of financial support for business-led research and development, providing over $3.84 billion annually in investment tax credits (ITCs) and income tax deductions across thousands of corporate and unincorporated claimants. According to CRA annual program statistics reported by Grantsights, 59% of SR&ED ITCs allowed in 2025–26 were refundable and 41% were non-refundable, with software development representing the largest single field at 42.6% of total ITCs allowed (up from 35.7% in 2021–22).

Between December 2024 and November 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most expansive structural overhaul since 2012. First, legislative amendments announced in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025—enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026—retroactively transformed the federal SR&ED regime for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024). These enacted reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual enhanced cash credit to $2.1 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), allowed Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) to elect into the revenue-based phase-out regime, and restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and capital lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Second, at the provincial level, Québec abolished seven legacy R&D and design tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating its innovation incentives into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)—a fully refundable credit providing 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on excess expenditures regardless of corporate asset size. Concurrently, British Columbia enacted Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026, making its 10% B.C. SR&ED tax credit permanent and harmonizing with the federal $6 million expenditure limit, ECPC access, and capital expenditure restoration, while Ontario updated its 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) to include 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024. Third, as of April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks (valid for up to three years) and halving post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 days to 90 days. Finally, as reported in industry analyses of Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026), the federal government proposed a $930 million five-year expansion ($235 million ongoing) extending federal SR&ED eligibility to regulatory/certification testing and intellectual property (IP) protection costs for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution of the SR&ED Regime
1.1 Dual-Incentive Structure under the Income Tax Act

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program is not a discretionary grant fund with a capped annual budget; it is a statutory entitlement embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that performs eligible SR&ED work and satisfies the statutory filing deadlines is legally entitled to two distinct, complementary tax incentives:

items: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (ITA Section 37): Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer (including a business actively carried on by a related corporation, such as a parent or subsidiary, at the time the expenditure is made). Expenditures added to the Section 37 pool may be deducted in whole or in part when calculating net business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely in a running pool balance to offset taxable business income in any future taxation year. For current SR&ED expenditures carried on outside Canada, subsection 37(2) permits a direct current-year deduction in computing business income, though foreign expenditures (aside from limited permissible Canadian-resident employee salaries under subsection 37(1.5)) cannot enter the Section 37 pool, cannot be claimed on Form T661, and do not earn investment tax credits.

The SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITA Sections 127 and 127.1): Under subsections 127(5) to 127(36) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a statutory percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Depending on the taxpayer's legal classification and expenditure type, earned ITCs are first applied to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5), and any remaining balance may either be refunded in cash under section 127.1 or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years.

body.text: To prevent double tax relief on the same dollar of expenditure, the two mechanisms are statutorily linked through a recapture-into-income ("grind") mechanism. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(v) of the Income Tax Act, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed to reduce Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund in Year 1 reduces the claimant's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 (reported on Line 435 of Form T661). If this reduction causes the Section 37 deductible pool balance to become negative at the end of Year 2, the negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(v).
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Every federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax claim in Canada stands or falls on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (which generally conforms to the OECD Frascati Manual). Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of four eligible categories—paragraphs (a) through (d)—while avoiding seven explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view—for example, laboratory studies of a newly discovered virus to characterize its molecular structure and properties, often resulting in peer-reviewed scientific publications. Under paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view—for example, investigating immunological mechanisms to develop a vaccine that exploits specific characteristics of a newly discovered virus. Under paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto—for example, scaling up and optimizing bioprocessing parameters to enable rapid, large-scale manufacturing of a vaccine where existing technological knowledge is insufficient. Experimental development is the most frequently claimed category in Canada, often referred to in jurisprudence as "shop floor SR&ED".

In addition to core research and experimental development, paragraph 248(1)(d) includes support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs (corresponding in amount, size, extent, or duration to what is strictly necessary) and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. To qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), support work must fall within one of eight exhaustive statutory categories:

items: Engineering;
Design;
Operations research;
Mathematical analysis;
Computer programming;
Data collection;
Testing; or
Psychological research.

body.text: On its own, paragraph (d) work—such as standard professional engineering practice or computer programming—does not involve scientific or technological uncertainty and is not eligible as standalone SR&ED; it qualifies only when carried out specifically to perform and directly support related paragraph (a), (b), or (c) work undertaken in Canada.
Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the Income Tax Act explicitly exclude seven categories of work from the definition of SR&ED, meaning they can never be claimed:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion (including demonstrations, contests, samples, exhibitions, trade shows, giveaways, public relations, and merchandising);
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes; and
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's eligibility guidelines emphasize, the presence of an excluded activity (such as mineral prospecting or routine data collection) within a broader corporate project does not automatically taint or disqualify the entire project; rather, the statutory exclusions delineate where eligible SR&ED stops and ineligible commercial or routine work begins, requiring strict cost segregation. What distinguishes eligible paragraph (d) support work (such as testing or data collection) from excluded paragraph (f) or (k) work (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose: whether the testing or data collection was performed specifically to support basic research, applied research, or experimental development, rather than to support normal commercial operations. Furthermore, activities aimed merely at acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists—such as employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—do not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve scientific or technological advancement and are ineligible.
1.3 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Framework

The administrative and judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) has evolved through four distinct historical phases. Prior to 1985, administrative guidance under Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 proved insufficient to explain the boundary between routine product development and eligible research and development. In the May 23, 1985 federal budget papers, the Department of Finance announced amendments adding the term "experimental development" to confirm that projects consisting solely of "routine engineering or routine development" were excluded. Following a March 4, 1986 confirmation from the Department of Finance that qualifying R&D must embody scientific or technological advancement, contain elements of scientific or technological uncertainty, and be conducted in a systematic and organized fashion, Revenue Canada and industry leaders co-developed Information Circular 86-4 (IC 86-4) in 1986 (updated through IC 86-4R3 in 1994 and supplemented by a December 2, 1992 clarification). IC 86-4 established the three foundational pillars of SR&ED: (1) scientific or technological advancement, (2) scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) scientific and technical content.

In the landmark 1998 decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (T.C.C.), Judge Donald Bowman synthesized IC 86-4R3 and the statutory text into a five-part judicial approach, which the Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed as a five-question framework in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393. In 2012 (revised April 24, 2015, and archived in August 2021), the CRA codified Judge Bowman's framework into five explicit questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy:

items: Question 1: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Question 2: Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Question 3: Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Question 4: Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Question 5: Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: On August 13, 2021, following a modernization initiative launched in 2020, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the statutory text of subsection 248(1) did not change, the 2021 Guidelines consolidated the five questions into two overarching requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—to establish a simplified common language for claimants and CRA officials.

The "Why" Requirement (consolidating Questions 1 and 4) mandates that the work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. Advancement refers to generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories, technological principles, or prediction models) that moves the understanding of science or technology forward, rather than merely acquiring factual knowledge (such as routine measurements) or achieving practical business benefits. New knowledge is needed only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—that is, when an insufficiency in the existing scientific or technological knowledge base (combining internal corporate resources and publicly available knowledge at the start of the project) makes it unknown or uncertain whether a given objective or result can be achieved. According to the CRA's guidelines, eight key characteristics signal that available technological knowledge is insufficient: existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; there are too many variables or unknowns; parameters or conditions fall outside normal operating ranges; the nature of the problem is evolving; data is not readily available; there are interlocking constraints; or economic/cost targets force the exploration of technologically uncertain pathways. If a problem is circumvented using a workaround based on existing knowledge, or if a novel product is created without resolving technological uncertainty (for example, testing supplier powders to mould a glow-in-the-dark potato peeler handle without altering the moulding process or plastic properties), no technological advancement occurs. Conversely, actual success in achieving project goals is never required: proving through experiment or analysis why a hypothesized technical solution will not succeed—and thereby rejecting a hypothesis and eliminating an unviable pathway—constitutes a valid scientific or technological advancement.

The "How" Requirement (consolidating Questions 2, 3, and 5) mandates that the work be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The CRA specifies that a systematic investigation requires more than merely taking an organized approach or following established engineering protocols; it must include four explicit sequential steps:

items: Defining a problem;
Advancing a hypothesis (an idea, proposed method, or possible solution consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for investigation) towards resolving that problem;

Planning and testing the hypothesis by means of experiment (structured tests/studies exploring relationships between variables) or analysis (detailed examination using models, graphs, or mathematical formulas), allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively; and
Developing logical conclusions based on the results while keeping contemporaneous records generated as the work progresses.

body.text: In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed that notwithstanding the CRA's administrative shift toward simplified terminology, the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the binding judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. As the Tax Court of Canada demonstrated in Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC 29, the two frameworks map seamlessly onto one another: Questions 1 and 4 establish the "Why," while Questions 2, 3, and 5 establish the "How".
1.4 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) and Budget 2026
Tax auditors and corporate claimants must distinguish between two waves of federal legislative reform enacted and announced between December 2024 and November 2026:
Wave 1: 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025 (Enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026)

Initially proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (which had originally proposed a $4.5 million expenditure limit and a $1.9 billion six-year investment) and expanded in Budget 2025, these reforms were formally legislated in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 enacted four major statutory changes:

items: Doubling of the Expenditure Limit: The maximum annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate doubled from $3 million to $6 million.

Expansion of Phase-Out Thresholds and Revenue Election: For Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range expanded from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million. Furthermore, under subsection 127(10.32) of the Income Tax Act, CCPCs (or associated groups of CCPCs) may now elect on a prescribed form to have their expenditure limit phase-out determined using the three-year average gross revenue formula instead of taxable capital, preventing capital-intensive scale-ups with high investor equity or debt from prematurely losing the 35% rate.

Extension of the 35% Enhanced Rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Under amended subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.6), public corporations resident in Canada, listed on a designated stock exchange, and not controlled directly or indirectly by non-residents now qualify for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6 million of annual qualified expenditures, phased out when average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15 million and $75 million (shared across consolidated group members).

Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Capital Leases: Reversing the 2012 Federal Budget repeal (which had excluded capital costs starting January 1, 2014), Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of depreciable capital property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, for both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 ITC (including all-or-substantially-all capital assets, First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment, and equipment lease payments), while eliminating the former subsection 37(14) capital look-through reduction for post-December 15, 2024 contracts and third-party payments.

body.text: Wave 2: Federal Budget 2026 (Tabled November 5, 2026) — Commercialization and IP Expansion

According to advisory analyses of Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026), the federal government proposed a $930 million expansion over five years (with $235 million ongoing) to extend the federal SR&ED program into downstream commercialization for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026. First, regulatory and certification work—comprising tests, technical validations, and studies performed to satisfy regulatory requirements for the initial approval or certification of a new or improved product—would qualify for SR&ED, provided the work relates directly to an underlying project that is already eligible under existing SR&ED rules, with eligible costs following standard categories (wages, materials, contract costs, overhead, and machinery or equipment). Second, intellectual property (IP) protection costs—comprising costs to obtain and maintain patents, plant breeders' rights, and registered copyrights in software (including preparing and filing applications and periodic maintenance fees in Canada or abroad, provided the support activities occur in Canada)—would qualify if the IP stems from eligible SR&ED work, excluding litigation and enforcement costs and subject to ITC recapture rules if the IP is subsequently sold.
2. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Outs, and Carryovers
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates by Claimant Type

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates on a two-tier volume-based rate structure under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act. The basic ITC rate of 15% is calculated on the excess of the claimant’s SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year over any provincial "super-allowance benefit amounts". The 15% basic rate applies to all corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large public corporations exceeding the revenue threshold), to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit, to sole proprietorships (individuals) and beneficiaries of trusts, and to partnerships. Because a partnership is not a "person" or "taxpayer" under the Income Tax Act, the SR&ED ITC is computed at the partnership level solely at the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(8) and allocated to eligible partners—even if a partner receiving the allocation is a CCPC or qualifying corporation.

The enhanced ITC rate of 35%—which consists of the 15% basic rate plus a 20% statutory enhancement under subsection 127(10.1)—is earned on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit ($3 million for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024; $6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) by two categories of corporate claimants:

items: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) as defined in subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act (private corporations resident in Canada that are not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, one or more public corporations, or any combination thereof); and

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) as defined in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: public corporations resident in Canada and listed on a designated stock exchange, where even if all the shares owned by non-residents were instead owned by a particular person, the corporation would still not be controlled directly or indirectly by that particular person).

body.text: 2.2 Expenditure Limits and Phase-Out Mechanics (Pre- and Post-December 16, 2024)

The maximum annual expenditure limit on which a CCPC (and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an ECPC) can earn the 35% enhanced ITC is governed by subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act. Stand-alone CCPCs calculate their expenditure limit on Schedule T2SCH31, whereas associated CCPCs must calculate a single group expenditure limit and allocate it amongst themselves using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Similarly, members of a consolidated group of ECPCs must calculate their expenditure limit using the group's average revenue and share that single limit among all members included in the consolidated financial statements.

Short Taxation Years and Multiple Year-Ends in a Calendar Year

Under subsection 127(10.5) of the Income Tax Act, if a corporation has a short taxation year (or has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC), its expenditure limit (or allocated share of an associated group's expenditure limit) must be prorated based on the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365. For example, as illustrated in Section 3.1 of the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if Corporation P is allocated $3,000,000 of an associated group's expenditure limit but has a short taxation year of 184 days running from July 1 to December 31, 2027, its expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is prorated to $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,328.
2.3 Refundability Rules, Qualifying Corporations, and the Qualifying Income Limit

Once an SR&ED ITC is earned, subsection 127(5) requires that it first be applied to reduce the taxpayer's federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the taxation year. Whether any remaining unapplied current-year ITC is paid out as a cash refund depends on section 127.1 (subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)) of the Income Tax Act, which differentiates between entity types and between current expenditures (and the Prescribed Proxy Amount) versus capital expenditures.

First, a CCPC that is a "Qualifying Corporation" (and not an "Excluded Corporation") enjoys the broadest refundability. Under subsection 127.1(2), a Qualifying Corporation is a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their preceding taxation years) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. A Qualifying Corporation (other than an excluded corporation) receives a 100% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on current-nature qualified expenditures and the PPA up to its expenditure limit, a 40% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital-nature qualified expenditures up to its expenditure limit, and a 40% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of its 15% basic ITC earned on both current and capital qualified expenditures over its expenditure limit.

Second, for a CCPC that is neither a Qualifying Corporation nor an Excluded Corporation (i.e., a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit, but whose prior-year taxable capital or three-year average revenue is below $75,000,000 so it retains an expenditure limit), the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC up to the expenditure limit remains 100% refundable on current expenditures (and PPA) and 40% refundable on capital expenditures, but any 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures over the expenditure limit is non-refundable.

Third, for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) in taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the refundability profile matches that of non-qualifying CCPCs: the 35% enhanced ITC earned up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is 100% refundable on current expenditures (and PPA) and 40% refundable on capital expenditures, while any 15% basic ITC earned above the expenditure limit is non-refundable.

Fourth, for an Excluded Corporation (a CCPC that is a Qualifying Corporation, but is also an excluded corporation under subsection 127.1(2)), the refund rate is 40% across all categories—40% on the 35% enhanced ITC (both current and capital) up to the expenditure limit, and 40% on the 15% basic ITC (both current and capital) over the expenditure limit.

Fifth, All Other Corporations (foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-ECPC public corporations, and CCPCs/ECPCs above the $75,000,000 phase-out threshold) earn only the 15% basic ITC, which is completely non-refundable. Finally, Individuals (other than trusts), Qualifying Trusts (where each beneficiary is a qualifying corporation or an individual), and Eligible Partners of a Partnership earn the 15% basic ITC and receive a 40% cash refund of their unclaimed current-year ITC after offsetting Part I tax payable (note, however, that an ITC allocated from a partnership to a corporate partner that is not a Qualifying Corporation cannot be refunded).

body.text: 2.5 Carryback, Carryforward, Taxability of Credits, and Acquisition of Control Restrictions

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs (or refundable ITCs that a claimant chooses not to have refunded) may be carried back up to 3 prior taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in those years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9). Any ITC that is applied against Part I tax payable or refunded in cash is subtracted from the available ITC pool and reduces the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e) (reported on Line 435 of Form T661), with any resulting negative pool balance included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(v).

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust experiences a change in majority-interest beneficiary)—a loss restriction event—there is a deemed taxation year-end immediately before the event. Under subsection 37(6.1), the corporation's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil, and the undeducted pre-acquisition pool balance may be reinstated and deducted in subsequent taxation years only if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the corporation's income for the year (before making any pool deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business. Parallel streaming restrictions apply to the carryforward of pre-acquisition unused ITCs and the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs.
3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method Election

When completing Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must choose each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (Line 160, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Income Tax Act) or the Traditional Method (Line 162, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the Act).

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant must specifically identify, track, and substantiate all overhead and other expenditures (reported on Line 360 of Form T661) that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Those actual overhead expenditures are added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and also earn ITCs. Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661; instead, actual overhead expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses. In lieu of actual overhead, the claimant calculates a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), equal to 55% of the eligible "Salary Base" of employees directly engaged in SR&ED—and includes this notional PPA (on Line 502 of Form T661) in its qualified SR&ED expenditures solely for the purpose of calculating Investment Tax Credits. Neither the PPA nor the overhead expenditures it represents can be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged, Specified Employees, and Foreign Work

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" is defined via subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act as income from an office or employment. It includes base salary, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay (excluding extended vacation or sick leave beyond normal annual entitlements), pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducement or non-competition payments treated as employment remuneration, and taxable benefits under section 6 of the Act (for cash outlays, or for non-cash benefits where the value is a reasonable estimate of actual cost, excludes GST/HST/PST unless no input tax credit is claimable, and is not deducted twice as a business expense). Conversely, dividends, stock option benefits (excluded because they do not represent an expenditure incurred by the employer), retiring allowances (excluded under subsection 248(1), though potentially claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), employer shares of related benefits (CPP, QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, pension plans, group medical/dental insurance), and partnership distributions to partners can never be claimed as SR&ED salaries or wages.
"Directly Engaged" vs. Administrative Support and the All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) Rule

Whether an employee's remuneration qualifies as direct SR&ED salary or wages depends on the tasks actually performed, not the employee's job title. Under the Proxy Method, only employees who are "directly engaged" in SR&ED qualify. The CRA defines "directly engaged" strictly as "hands-on" work in basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work: conducting experiments or analyses, preparing equipment or materials for experiments (excluding routine maintenance), recording measurements, making calculations, preparing charts/graphs, carrying out statistical surveys, or writing computer programs. First-line managers and supervisors are considered "directly engaged" only for the hours spent directly guiding the technical aspects of the investigation or providing direct technical input; time spent on non-technological management, administrative duties, or commercial decision-making is excluded. Clerical and administrative personnel (accounting, human resources, payroll, reception, shipping) are never directly engaged under the Proxy Method, though their salaries may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental to SR&ED. Work performed by non-specialized employees qualifies only if it is directly in support of, and an integral part of, the research or experimental development and is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Under the All or Substantially All (ASA) rule (subsection 2900(5) of the Income Tax Regulations), if a non-specified employee spends 90% or more of their time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be included; otherwise, only the reasonable proportion of time relating to SR&ED may be claimed.
Rules and Statutory Caps for "Specified Employees"

Under the Income Tax Act and CRA policy, a "specified employee" is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly (alone or together with non-arm's length persons), a significant interest (10% or more of the issued shares of any class) in the corporation or a related corporation. Founders and owner-managers of CCPCs are typically specified employees.

The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose two layers of restrictions on specified employees. First, in computing allowable SR&ED salary or wages for the Section 37 deductible pool (Lines 305 and 309 of Form T661), bonuses and remuneration based on profits are strictly excluded for specified employees (whereas bonuses and profit-based remuneration are included for non-specified employees on Line 300), and the total deductible SR&ED salary (including taxable benefits and prior-year unpaid salary paid in the year) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE). Second, in computing the Salary Base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Part 5, Lines 850–860 of Form T661) under subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, taxable benefits, bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and prior-year unpaid wages are excluded for all employees, and the amount included in the PPA Salary Base for each specified employee (Box 860) is restricted to the lesser of:

body.text: Unpaid Remuneration (180-Day Rule under Subsection 78(4)) and Foreign SR&ED Salaries (Subsection 37(1.5))

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year; it must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 and can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (and can never enter the PPA Salary Base).

Under subsection 37(1.5) of the Income Tax Act, salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (Lines 307 and 309) may be claimed on Form T661 if: (1) the employee was a resident of Canada; (2) the foreign work was solely in support of SR&ED carried on by the claimant in Canada; and (3) the remuneration was not subject to an income or profits tax from another country. The allowable foreign SR&ED salary is capped at the lesser of the actual eligible foreign salary paid or 10% of the total Canadian SR&ED salary or wages incurred in the taxation year.
3.3 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Calculation and Overall Cap

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method on Line 160, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated on Line 820 in Part 5 of Form T661 pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations as 55% of the total Salary Base (Line 818), where the Salary Base is the sum of eligible non-specified employee base wages (Line 814) and capped specified employee base wages (Line 816). (Historical PPA rates were 65% for 2012 and prior years and 60% for 2013; since 2014, the rate has been 55%).

However, the calculated PPA is subject to the Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations, which ensures that the sum of qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specified deductions under the Income Tax Act does not exceed the total business expenditures deducted in the taxation year. Under Regulation 2900(6), the Overall Cap is calculated as:
A − B − C

where A is the total of all amounts deducted in calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold, adjusted per Schedule T2SCH1); B is the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance on Schedule T2SCH8, interest, and bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance brokers), 37 (the SR&ED deduction claimed in the year on Line 460 of Form T661 / Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development), and 104 (trusts) of the Income Tax Act; and C is the total of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent). As the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy notes, the Overall Cap generally does not restrict the PPA for claimants carrying on a diversified business or deducting more than $55 of non-SR&ED, non-rent, non-CCA operating expenses for each $100 of eligible salary in the Salary Base.
3.4 Overhead and Other Current Expenditures (Traditional Method)

If a claimant chooses the Traditional Method on Line 162 of Form T661, it claims actual SR&ED overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 pursuant to subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Income Tax Act and paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations. Per the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an expenditure under Regulation 2900(2)(c) must satisfy both tests of the "directly attributable" framework:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect straight to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada without an intervening step or intermediary, demonstrating a direct linkage to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED. General corporate administration, management, and "overhead on overhead" have an indirect relationship and fail this test.

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred. Fixed costs—such as routine monthly base charges for telephone, cellular phone, or standard business internet services, or fixed-cost maintenance contracts that would be incurred regardless of SR&ED—fail the incremental test and are ineligible (whereas long-distance charges, incremental utilities, incremental active-project waste disposal, clinical trial volunteer fees, Canadian SR&ED travel/lodging/training, scientific periodical subscriptions, and moving costs to relocate SR&ED staff within Canada can qualify).

body.text: With respect to cloud computing, dedicated bandwidth, and software, the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) confirms that dedicated bandwidth costs incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify as an allowable lease of equipment even under the Proxy Method (provided they are dedicated for SR&ED and are not general-purpose office equipment), following Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877. Similarly, under the post-December 15, 2024 capital and lease restoration, fees for software and cloud space used directly for experimentation and development can qualify under the applicable capital, lease, or overhead provisions.

Even where certain expenses are deductible in the Section 37 pool under the Traditional Method, section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations designates specific "prescribed expenditures" that must be deducted on Line 530 of Form T661 and never earn Investment Tax Credits. Under Regulation 2902, prescribed expenditures include: general administrative or management costs; legal or accounting fees (including fees for preparing SR&ED claims); interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g); entertainment, advertising, or selling expenses; conference or convention attendance costs; dues or fees for membership in a scientific or technical society; fines or penalties; maintenance and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment not directly attributable to SR&ED; expenditures for the acquisition of used equipment; and expenditures to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (subject to the IP expansion proposed in Budget 2026 for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026).
3.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Production Runs

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) (Traditional Method), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, claimants under both calculation methods may claim the laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs/excise duties, transportation, acquisition, and storage) or production cost of physical, tangible materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials (which include raw materials, substances in solid, liquid, or gaseous state, and animals or plants/fertilizers used in testing) may be acquired from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided they are actually consumed or transformed in Canada during the taxation year (not merely held in inventory) and paid for within 180 days of the taxation year-end under subsection 127(26). For materials purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes (adjusted on Line 542) to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier, excluding any intercompany profit element.

Per the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, materials consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during the prosecution of SR&ED. If experimental production is sold as scrap for 10% or less of its original cost, the input materials are accepted as "materials consumed" and no ITC recapture applies; if sold for more than 10% of original cost, the input materials are considered not to have been consumed. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials changed in character, form, or structure, or incorporated into another product or asset as part of SR&ED, that are not rendered virtually valueless. While 100% of the cost of materials transformed is claimable in the year of transformation, subsection 127(27) ITC recapture applies if the resulting product, prototype, or asset is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years.

When SR&ED occurs alongside asset development, the CRA distinguishes four asset categories: (1) Pilot plants (non-commercial scale facilities developed and operated over their useful life solely for SR&ED, never intended for temporary or permanent commercial conversion); (2) Commercial plants (where only current SR&ED costs to resolve technological uncertainties qualify, and non-SR&ED commercial costs must be isolated); (3) Prototypes (original trial models built to test a hypothesis and lacking lasting value, where duplicate copies qualify as materials only if constructed and tested strictly to support SR&ED prior to commercial production); and (4) Custom products or commercial assets. Similarly, under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, when experimental development occurs during commercial facility trial runs (ED+EP), labour, overhead, and material costs relating to excess or commercial production are excluded. When SR&ED is embedded within a custom product or commercial asset and it is impossible for both the claimant and the CRA to isolate the SR&ED work, the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy permits an administrative Alternative Approach:

Allowable SR&ED expenditures = (total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset − estimated costs that would usually be associated with constructing the asset if the technology had already existed) + estimated cost of materials transformed in SR&ED

To use this formula, both the claimant and the CRA must agree that cost isolation is impossible, and the claimant must sign a formal waiver of its right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the Income Tax Act.
3.6 Subcontractors, Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, when a claimant contracts an arm's-length party to perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work in Canada on the claimant's behalf (Line 340), 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, but only 80% qualifies for the Investment Tax Credit (a 20% reduction is subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661). To earn an ITC on Line 340, the contracted SR&ED work must be performed in Canada by a taxable supplier (payments to non-taxable suppliers are removed on Line 528, and foreign contractor costs cannot be claimed on Form T661, though they are deductible under subsection 37(2)), and must be paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end under subsection 127(26) (unpaid contract invoices are deducted on Line 520 and added back on Line 500 at 80% when paid in a later year). For the contractor (performer), any contract payment received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis (Line 517) so that both parties do not claim ITCs on the same work. Furthermore, while an arm's-length payer can claim a contract for eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work (provided it is commensurate with and directly supports the payer's Canadian SR&ED), an arm's-length contractor performing only support work cannot claim SR&ED ITCs on its own return because support work on its own is not SR&ED. Following Bill C-15's restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, the CRA's updated June 2026 SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy confirms that contract expenditures and third-party payments made after December 15, 2024, are generally no longer reduced by non-current expenditures of the performer under the former subsection 37(14) capital look-through rule.

When a claimant contracts a non-arm's-length (NAL) party to perform SR&ED on its behalf (Line 345), the contract expenditure enters the payer's Section 37 deductible pool, but does not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer, nor does the payment reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures as a contract payment. Instead, the NAL performer either claims the ITC itself (including for support work performed for the NAL payer) or—under subsection 127(13) of the Income Tax Act—both parties jointly execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's net qualified expenditures (including its PPA, capped at the contract amount and stripped of intercompany profit) to the payer (Line 544 for the performer; Line 508 for the payer). Under subsection 127(24), an anti-avoidance rule prevents taxpayers from circumventing NAL contract rules by inserting an arm's-length intermediary between a payer and a NAL performer.

Distinct from SR&ED contracts performed on behalf of a claimant, Third-Party Payments (Line 370, governed by subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) and reported on Form T1263) are payments made to approved associations (B Entities, clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(A)), approved universities, affiliated colleges, or other CRA-approved colleges/research institutes (C Entities, clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(B)), tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j) (D and F Entities), or approved granting councils such as NSERC, CIHR, and SSHRC (E Entities, clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)) for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant's business where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Like arm's-length contracts, third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for the federal ITC (subject to the 20% reduction on Line 529).
3.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted via Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and detailed in the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), capital property and lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, once again qualify for SR&ED tax incentives under three specific regimes:

items: Full SR&ED Capital Expenditures — The ASA (≥90%) Test (Line 390): Under paragraph 37(1)(b), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III), and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, expenditures to acquire new or used depreciable property that becomes available for use (under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, qualify for 100% inclusion on Line 390 of Form T661 if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that the property would either: (a) be used all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (b) have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed to perform SR&ED in Canada (including property used in asset development that has less than 10% remaining life expectancy or less than 10% remaining value afterward). New ASA depreciable property qualifies for both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 ITC (where capital ITCs up to the expenditure limit are 40% refundable for CCPCs and ECPCs), whereas used depreciable property qualifies on Line 390 for the Section 37 deductible pool only and must be deducted on Line 530 as a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) so it does not earn an ITC. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance), and land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings remain strictly excluded.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) — The >50% ("Primarily") Actual Operating Time Test (Line 504): Under subsection 127(9) and the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), new depreciable equipment acquired (available for use) after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test (and is not used equipment, general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), or Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) intended at acquisition for commercial plant assembly/commissioning and primarily non-SR&ED use over its useful life) qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible pool; its capital cost remains on Schedule T2SCH8 and is depreciated under standard CCA rules (with any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reducing the class's Undepreciated Capital Cost in the subsequent taxation year under subsections 13(7.1) and 13(7.4)). If the new equipment is actually used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "first period" (from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition), 25% (1/4) of its capital cost qualifies for the ITC on Line 504 as First-Term SUE. If it qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be used primarily (>50% of operating time) for SR&ED from acquisition through the end of the "second period" (the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost qualifies for the ITC on Line 504 as Second-Term SUE.

Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024): Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify according to the claimant's elected method. Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF and buildings) is used ASA (≥90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily (>50% to <90%) of its operating time for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); and if used ≤50% of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% is claimable. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ASA (≥90%), 100% is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), and if used <90%, the proportional percentage of total operating time used in SR&ED is claimable on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c)). Building rent remains excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada under Regulation 2903, while land lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are allowable under the Traditional Method (if ASA or directly attributable) but excluded under the Proxy Method.

body.text: 3.8 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant acquired a property (such as materials transformed, a prototype, ASA capital equipment, or Shared-Use Equipment) in the current taxation year or any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years by subsection 127(36)), the cost of the property was a qualified expenditure included in computing the claimant's ITC, and the claimant subsequently disposes of the property (or a product incorporating the property) or converts it to commercial use, the claimant must recapture all or part of the ITC by adding the recaptured amount to its Part I tax payable in the year of disposition or conversion.

The recapture amount added to Part I tax payable under subsection 127(27) is calculated by multiplying the historical ITC rate at which the original credit was earned on that property by the lesser of: (1) the original qualified expenditure (cost) of the property, and (2) either the proceeds of disposition (if disposed of to an arm's-length person) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's-length party). Recapture does not apply to internal salaries, wages, or overhead incurred to manufacture a property, nor does it apply under the 10% de minimis rule where scrap sales proceeds or FMV upon conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property. Under subsections 127(33) to 127(35), transferring SR&ED capital property to a non-arm's-length purchaser does not trigger immediate recapture if the purchaser maintains ASA SR&ED use, shifting any future recapture obligation to the NAL purchaser. Any ITC recapture added to Part I tax payable in Year 1 is added back to increase the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 (Line 453 of Form T661).
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
4.1 Interaction Between Provincial/Territorial Credits and Federal SR&ED

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer R&D tax credits (only Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit). Under paragraph 12(1)(x), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (whether refundable or non-refundable) constitute "government assistance" for federal SR&ED purposes. Consequently, provincial R&D tax credits reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (on Lines 513–514 of Form T661) in the taxation year in which the provincial credit is earned, prior to multiplying by the 35% or 15% federal ITC rate.

Special Audit Rule for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): As set out in Section 4.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional 55% PPA reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(18) (on Line 513/514), but is NOT deducted from the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) (on Line 429). Because the PPA is a notional amount that was never added to the Section 37 deductible pool, the portion of the provincial credit relating to the PPA (as well as any legacy Québec credit earned on support salaries or subcontract portions not eligible under the federal Proxy Method) must instead be included directly in taxable business income in the year received under paragraph 12(1)(x). Furthermore, in British Columbia (for non-refundable credits), Manitoba, Nova Scotia, and Ontario (under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007), a taxpayer may formally renounce or waive a provincial R&D tax credit if it wishes to avoid grinding down its 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC.
4.2 Comprehensive Jurisdiction-by-Jurisdiction Analysis
1. Québec — Transition to the New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

Administered by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec), Québec's R&D tax system underwent a fundamental restructuring announced in the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6, detailed in Revenu Québec's July 9, 2025 Tax News and official July 7, 2026 guidelines).

For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning before March 26, 2025, claimants continued to claim Québec's four legacy refundable R&D tax credits (enclosed with Form RD-222-V, Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures): (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V), (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, requiring a qualification certificate from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy), and (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, where cumulative fee balances at the end of a tax year ending after March 25, 2025, remain claimable for tax years ending no later than December 31, 2029). For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated all four legacy R&D credits, along with three additional measures: the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, the industrial design component of the design tax credits (while retaining the fashion design component), and the personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

Replacing those abolished measures for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, is the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed by eligible corporations (and corporate members of partnerships) operating a business with an establishment in Québec by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Form RD-1029.8.CR) with the Québec corporate income tax return. The CRIC is 100% refundable regardless of the corporation's asset size or CCPC status, paying 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold and 20% on qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 cap.

While the R&D component of the CRIC is harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED (and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC also covers eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with (as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including quality control work strictly related to implementing a quality control system required for initial certification), and (2) product design (including form and aesthetics development, functional improvements, prototype development, pilot user validation, and selection of materials). If the underlying R&D was performed outside Québec, subsequent pre-commercialization work in Québec fails the continuity requirement and does not qualify.

Qualified CRIC expenditures incurred in Québec comprise: 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for an eligible contract carried out in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital equipment) used for eligible work in Québec (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and excluding property claimed under the C3i investment and innovation credit or a large investment project tax holiday). Before applying the 30% and 20% rates, qualified expenditures must exceed an annual applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount (BPA) under the Québec personal income tax system for each employee ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026), prorated by the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Complementing the CRIC, Québec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI / DCI) provides a reduced effective Québec corporate income tax rate of 2% on qualified income from commercializing Québec-developed IP, with its Québec nexus ratio updated after March 25, 2025, to reference R&D expenditures eligible for the CRIC (excluding pre-commercialization expenses and without deducting the CRIC exclusion threshold).
2. Ontario — Three-Pillar Corporate R&D Tax Credit System

Administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) (S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A), Ontario provides three corporate R&D tax credits for corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment that file a federal Form T661.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule T2SCH566) is an 8% fully refundable tax credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; 10% prior to June 1, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), yielding a maximum annual refund of $240,000 (entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5). Per the official Ontario government update of October 30, 2026, qualified OITC expenditures include 100% of current expenditures (salaries, 55% PPA, materials, 80% of arm's-length contracts) and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (capital expenditures between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, were excluded, while pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40%). The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is gradually reduced if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule T2SCH508) is a 3.5% non-refundable credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap, carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Because Ontario law treats the OITC as government assistance for ORDTC purposes (whereas neither the federal ITC nor the ORDTC reduces the OITC base), the 3.5% ORDTC is calculated on eligible Ontario expenditures after subtracting the 8% OITC—producing an effective ORDTC rate of 3.22% (3.5% × 92%) and a combined Ontario rate of 11.22% before grinding the federal SR&ED pool.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules T2SCH568 and T2SCH569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence) up to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20,000,000 shared among associated corporations (a maximum cash refund of $4,000,000 per year, entered on Line 470 of Schedule 5).
3. British Columbia — Permanent Credit and 2026 Alignment with Federal Reforms

Administered by the CRA under Part 6 (Sections 97 to 103) of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia) and claimed on Form T666 within 18 months of the corporate tax year-end, the B.C. SR&ED tax credit was made permanent by Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), which also aligned B.C.'s regime with the federal Bill C-15 changes effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Under the 2026 rules, both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn a 10% fully refundable credit (Line 674 of Schedule 5) on B.C. qualified expenditures (including restored capital expenditures) up to the increased $6,000,000 expenditure limit (a maximum annual refund of $600,000, up from $300,000), phased out for prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average revenue for ECPCs) between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Expenditures above the limit, and expenditures by other qualifying corporations, earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Line 659 of Schedule 5) that carries back 3 years, carries forward 10 years, or may be renounced.
4. Alberta — Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Administered by the Province of Alberta under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (Information Circular IEG-1) and claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the corporation's filing due date (21 months after year-end), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a fully refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual eligible Alberta R&D spending (matching federal SR&ED expenditure definitions). The IEG pays 8% on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (defined as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous 2 taxation years), and an enhanced 20% on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the 2-year base spending level.
5. Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

In Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan), Sections 63 to 63.4 — Schedule T2SCH403, administered by the CRA), CCPCs earn a 10% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible annual Saskatchewan expenditures and a 10% non-refundable credit above $1,000,000, while non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years, with no recapture). Saskatchewan also offers the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) ("Patent Box"), reducing the provincial Corporate Income Tax rate to 6% for 10 years on qualifying commercialized innovation income.

In Manitoba (The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), Section 7.3 — Schedule T2SCH380, administered by the CRA with a filing deadline of 1 year after the filing due date), the credit rate is 15% of eligible Manitoba expenditures (20% prior to April 12, 2017). For in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years, with an election to renounce up to 1 year after the filing due date, or within 6 months of year-end for federal purposes). For R&D carried on in Manitoba under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute, the full 15% credit is 100% refundable (and contract payments to eligible Manitoba educational institutions are 100% eligible without the federal 80% restriction; Manitoba also protected its credit base from the 2014–2024 federal exclusion of capital expenditures).

In the Atlantic Provinces and Yukon (all administered by the CRA), Nova Scotia (Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), Section 41 — Schedule T2SCH340, filing deadline 18 months after corporate tax year-end, with a 6-month renunciation option), New Brunswick (New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Section 59 — Schedule T2SCH360, non-refundable carryback 3 years / carryforward 7 years where applicable, recapture applies), Newfoundland and Labrador (Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), Section 42 — Schedule T2SCH301 for corporations and Form T1129 for individuals, filing deadline 12 months after the filing due date), and Yukon (Income Tax Act (Yukon), Section 15 — Schedule T2SCH442 for corporations and Form T1232 for individuals, filing deadline 12 months after the filing due date) all provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no annual expenditure cap. Uniquely, in Newfoundland and Labrador, eligible provincial R&D expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits), although the resulting NL credit reduces the federal SR&ED pool.
