body.text: 5. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Statutory Deadlines
5.1 Governing Authorities and Institutional Division of Labour

Canada’s R&D tax incentive system is governed by a statutory division of responsibilities between policy formulation and tax administration. The Department of Finance Canada holds authority over tax policy, legislative drafting of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (including Part XXIX, Regulations 2900–2903), and the building-by-building approval of prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—through its Business Tax Incentives Directorate (headquartered at the Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5) and regional coordinating tax services offices in Surrey (BC), Toronto (ON), Laval (QC), and Halifax (NS)—administers both the scientific/technical review and the financial review of all federal SR&ED claims, as well as the provincial and territorial R&D tax credits for British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Saskatchewan, and Yukon. Revenu Québec and the Ministère des Finances du Québec administer the Québec CRIC (relying on the CRA for the scientific review of R&D work while administering Québec pre-commercialization and financial rules directly), and the Province of Alberta administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant.
5.2 Complete Architecture of Form T661 and Supplementary Prescribed Forms

To access federal SR&ED tax incentives, a claimant must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) (updated May 15, 2026) along with its income tax return (T1, T2, T3, or T5013 Partnership Information Return), together with the prescribed ITC form: Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporations or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for individuals and trusts. Depending on the claimant's corporate structure and transactions, Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 must be accompanied by supplementary prescribed forms: Schedule T2SCH49 (allocation of the expenditure limit among associated CCPCs), Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026), Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED), and Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED).
Form T661 is organized into structured parts that must contain all prescribed information by the reporting deadline:

items: Part 2 — Project Information (Lines 200 to 282): Must be completed on a project-by-project basis for all projects claimed, or at minimum the 20 largest projects in dollar value at the time of filing. Section A captures the project title and code (Line 200), start date (Line 202), completion or expected completion date (Line 204), Field of Science or Technology code from Guide T4088 Appendix 1 (Line 206), continuation claim history (Lines 208–210), and joint/collaborative business disclosures (Lines 218–221). Section B captures the core technical narratives required to establish eligibility: Line 242 (What technological obstacles/uncertainties did you have to overcome?), Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome those technological obstacles/uncertainties?), and Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244?). Section C records key personnel and their qualifications (Lines 253–261), foreign salary claims (Line 265), work performed on behalf of another party (Line 266), non-employee contractors and their Business Numbers (Lines 267–269), and the Supporting Evidence Checklist (Lines 270–282) identifying contemporaneous documentation (project planning documents, timesheets, experimental designs, CAD models, lab notebooks, source code/commit logs, trial run logs, progress reports, photographs/videos, and physical samples/scrap).

Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Lines 160 to 470): Section A captures the election to use the Proxy Method (Line 160) or Traditional Method (Line 162). Section B computes Allowable SR&ED Expenditures: Canadian non-specified wages (Line 300), Canadian specified employee wages (Line 305), foreign non-specified wages (Line 307), foreign specified wages (Line 309), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310), current-year wages unpaid after 180 days (Line 315), materials consumed (Line 320), materials transformed (Line 325), arm's-length contracts (Line 340), non-arm's-length contracts (Line 345), overhead and other expenditures under the Traditional Method (Line 360), third-party payments (Line 370), total current SR&ED expenditures (Line 380), capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (Line 390), and Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400). Section C computes the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures by deducting provincial government assistance (Line 429), other government assistance (Line 431), non-government assistance (Line 432), prior-year ITCs applied and/or refunded (Line 435), and capital asset sales/other deductions (Line 440), and adding assistance repayments (Line 445), prior-year pool balance (Line 450), amalgamation/wind-up transfers (Line 452), and prior-year ITC recapture (Line 453) to determine the Amount Available for Deduction (Line 455), the optional Deduction Claimed in the Year (Line 460), and the Pool Balance Carried Forward (Line 470).

Part 4 — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 500 to 570): Adds payment of prior-year unpaid non-wage amounts (Line 500, at 80% if for an arm's-length contract), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and qualified expenditures transferred in on Form T1146 (Line 508); then subtracts provincial, federal, and non-government assistance and contract payments (Lines 513–517), current non-wage expenditures unpaid after 180 days (Line 520), payments to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), the 20% reduction on arm's-length contracts and third-party payments (Line 529), prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 (Line 530), other deductions for tax-exempt income (Line 533), and NAL adjustments (Lines 538–544) to arrive at Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 559), assistance repayments (Line 560), and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Line 570) (reported on Lines 350 and 370 of Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or Line 6712 of Form T2038(IND) for individuals).

Part 5 — Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (Lines 810 to 860): Computes the non-specified employee salary base (Lines 810–814), the specified employee cap schedule (Lines 850–860 and Line 816), the total Salary Base (Line 818), and the 55% PPA (Line 820) subject to the Overall Cap.

Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) and Part 10 (Certification): Part 9 requires full disclosure of any paid claim preparer and billing arrangement code (contingency fee, hourly/daily rate, flat fee, or other), and Part 10 contains the irrevocable certification of the claimant's signing officer.

body.text: 5.3 Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Strict "Prescribed Information" Doctrine

Under subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1) (for the Section 37 expenditure pool) and paragraph 127(9)(m) (for the Section 127 ITC) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations (18 Months): Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, its SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, a December 31, 2025 year-end must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 on or before June 30, 2027).

Individuals (17.5 Months for Self-Employed): Because self-employed individuals have a T1 filing-due date of June 15 (April 30 for other individuals), adding 12 months yields an SR&ED reporting deadline of 17.5 months after the December 31 taxation year-end (June 15 of the second following year).

Partnerships: A partnership must file Form T661 with its Form T5013 Partnership Information Return no later than 12 months after the earliest filing-due date of any member (partner) for the taxation year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends, and each partner must file their own Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) by their own respective SR&ED reporting deadline.

body.text: Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, the CRA has zero statutory discretion to waive or extend the SR&ED reporting deadline under subsection 220(2.1) in respect of prescribed forms or prescribed information required under subsection 37(11) or paragraph 127(9)(m). Filing draft estimates or a letter of intent to file does not satisfy the Act. If a claimant files a multiple-project claim (e.g., 15 projects) before the deadline but includes Part 2 Project Descriptions for only 10 projects, the CRA will allow the 10 complete projects and disallow the 5 projects missing prescribed information unless the missing Part 2 descriptions are submitted on or before the 18-month reporting deadline. Similarly, if Form T661 is filed on time but Schedule T2SCH31 is filed after the 18-month deadline, the expenditures may enter the Section 37 deductible pool, but no ITC can be earned (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301).
5.4 Claim Preparer Disclosures (Part 9) and Civil/Criminal Penalty Regimes
The Income Tax Act enforces strict civil and criminal penalties for non-compliant or overstated SR&ED claims:

items: Claim Preparer Penalty (Subsection 162(5.1) — $1,000 Penalty): If Part 9 of Form T661 (disclosing the name and billing arrangement—contingency fee, hourly rate, or flat fee—of any person paid to prepare or assist in preparing the claim) is omitted, incomplete, or inaccurate, the claim is not disallowed, but subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty for which both the claimant and the paid preparer are jointly and severally liable.

Civil Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsections 163(2), 163(2.1), and 163(3)): Per the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), any person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED return is liable under subsection 163(2) (paragraphs 163(2)(a) and 163(2)(d)) to a civil penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of: (a) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (where subsection 163(2.1) deems a loss claimant's taxable income not to be less than zero so that theoretical Part I tax is calculated on overstated Section 37 deductions, and CRA ordering rules deem overstated pool deductions and overstated ITCs to be deducted first, including across carryback/carryforward years), plus (b) the entire refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed. Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. The CRA considers applying subsection 163(2) penalties where a claimant fabricates activities that did not take place, includes projects it clearly knew did not involve SR&ED, or repeatedly claims non-qualifying, miscalculated, or unsubstantiated amounts after receiving prior written notification from the CRA (where the amounts are not under objection or appeal).

Criminal Prosecution (Subsection 239(1.1)): Under paragraphs 239(1.1)(a), (c), (g), and (h) of the Income Tax Act, making false or misleading statements or entries in books or records to claim an SR&ED ITC refund is a criminal offence carrying a mandatory fine of 50% to 200% of the excess ITC claimed (even if the fraud is detected during audit and $0 is actually disbursed by the CRA) plus up to two years' imprisonment on summary conviction (R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora Inc., 2017 QCCQ 2684).

body.text: 6. CRA Administration, Pre-Claim Approval, Technical & Financial Reviews, and Dispute Resolution
6.1 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 2026)

Introduced in the Canada Strong Budget 2025 and available from the CRA as of April 1, 2026, the SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process is an optional upfront service that provides businesses with an official technical determination from the CRA within 8 weeks on whether their planned projects meet the definition of SR&ED before beginning work or incurring significant costs.

To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business must: (1) operate in Canada as a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership; (2) have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000; and (3) be in good standing with the CRA. Furthermore, the proposed project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under objection or litigation. The application proceeds in four steps:

items: Request a Case Number: Complete a brief (<5 minute) web form on Canada.ca; existing SR&ED claimants receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days, while new SR&ED claimants receive a phone call from the CRA within 5 business days.
Submit Application in My Business Account: Upload the application using existing project planning documents for up to 3 projects.

Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) within 4 Weeks: Within 4 weeks of submission, an assigned RTA conducts a 2-to-5-hour meeting (mandatory for new claimants; optional/as-needed for existing claimants in good standing) to review the state of technology, technological uncertainty, and planned systematic investigation.

Receive Official Determination within 8 Weeks (Valid for Up to 3 Years): Within 8 weeks of submitting the complete application, the CRA issues a Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If granted, pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years (unless material changes are made to the project), and when the claimant subsequently files its annual Form T661, if a claim containing pre-claim approved projects is selected for an expenditure-only review, the CRA processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

body.text: 6.2 CRA Service Standards, AI-Supported Risk Screening, and Review Triggers

Upon filing Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31, claims undergo AI-supported automated screening and risk assessment (or random sampling). Per the CRA's The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026) and 2025–26 program statistics:

items: Refundable Claims Accepted Without Review: Processed within a 60-calendar-day service standard (met on 95% of claims in 2025–26).
Pre-Claim Approved Claims Selected for Expenditure-Only Review: Processed within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim.

Refundable Claims Selected for Technical and/or Financial Review: Processed within a 180-calendar-day service standard from receipt of a complete claim, with a 90% compliance target (met on 92.5% of reviewed refundable claims in 2025–26).
Non-Refundable Claims Selected for Review: Not subject to a formal service standard.

body.text: Once a claim is selected for review, it can never be withdrawn because the certification signed in Part 10 of Form T661 is irrevocable.
6.3 Roles of the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR)

During a review, a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, or RTM) evaluates whether the work meets the subsection 248(1) eligibility criteria, while a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager, or FRM) audits whether the claimed expenditures are allowable. Reviews are assigned nationally and conducted primarily via videoconferencing (with on-site visits granted on an exceptional, case-by-case basis by review management). During the review meeting, reviewers interview the company personnel who actually performed or supervised the work, tour the facilities virtually or on-site, and inspect contemporaneous supporting evidence generated during the course of the work (noting explicitly that oral statements made during interviews are recorded in working papers but are not a substitute for adequate contemporaneous documentation). At the conclusion of the review, if adjustments or penalties are proposed, the CRA issues a written SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and a Proposal Letter, granting the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations and additional evidence prior to issuing a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment.
6.4 Four-Tier Escalation and Dispute Resolution Framework
Per the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025), claimants have access to a four-step escalation process:

items: Step 1 — Talk to the RTA and/or FR: Address factual misunderstandings or missing documentation directly with the reviewers during the review or within the 30-day proposal window.

Step 2 — Contact the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM): If concerns remain unresolved, involve the RTM and/or FRM to review the facts and positions of both parties before the file is closed.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532 to the Assistant Director, SR&ED): After receiving the written Proposal Package and before the file is closed, the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5), which forwards the request within 3 business days to the local Assistant Director, SR&ED. An Administrative Review is not a second technical or financial audit; it evaluates whether the claimant received due process and whether the review complied with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection to the CRA Appeals Branch (Form T400A within 90 Days) and Tax Court Appeal: Once the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 days from the date of mailing (paragraph 165(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act; extendable by at most 1 year under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5)) to file a formal Notice of Objection online via My Business Account / Represent a Client or by mailing Form T400A to the Chief of Appeals (large corporations with taxable capital over $10 million must specify each issue and relief sought in detail and pay 50% of disputed amounts upfront). If unresolved at the Appeals Branch, the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 7. Landmark Judicial Precedents and Case Law Analysis
Because subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is concise, Canadian SR&ED compliance is heavily shaped by jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
7.1 Foundational Eligibility and the Five-Question Framework

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (T.C.C.), the appellant engineering firm claimed SR&ED credits for physical hydraulic modelling and river engineering projects. Allowing the appeal in large part, Judge Donald Bowman established the five foundational criteria for SR&ED eligibility (discussed in Section 1.3) and defined technological uncertainty as something that "exists in the mind of the specialist" and cannot be removed by "routine engineering or standard procedures"—where routine engineering refers to techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (F.C.A.), the appellant developed custom multilingual software (International Distributed Lottery System) to process 25,000 daily lottery orders across 2–3 million customers. Affirming the Tax Court's dismissal of the claim, the Federal Court of Appeal (per Sexton J.A.) formally endorsed the five Northwest Hydraulic questions, holding that building a complex custom software system because off-the-shelf software is unavailable does not constitute SR&ED if the uncertainties can be resolved through standard software engineering, and that failing to call any witness directly involved in the software development (such as the project manager) justified an adverse inference against the taxpayer.

Two decades later, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246), and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47), corporate appellants argued that because the literal phrase "scientific method" does not appear in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (and was omitted from revised CRA administrative guidelines), the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion was ultra vires the statute. The Federal Court of Appeal (per Webb J.A. in Kam-Press and Rennie J.A. in National R&D) unanimously rejected this argument and dismissed both appeals, holding under Canada Trustco (2005 SCC 54) that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1), that non-binding CRA guidelines cannot override appellate precedent, and that vague software project-tracking records lacking methodical hypothesis testing fail subsection 248(1).
7.2 Contemporaneous Documentation, Oral Testimony, and the Repeatability Standard

In the early decision Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue, 88 DTC 1363 (T.C.C.), involving an abandoned mechanical project where test records were discarded, Judge Sarchuk held that "systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments and of highly accurate measurements" and required documentary test records enabling third-party repeatability. In Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724 (T.C.C.), Judge Bowman tempered that rigid approach in a textile R&D case, emphasizing that Section 37 is designed to encourage real-world industrial R&D in Canada (while also holding that unprincipled audit compromise settlements bind neither the Minister nor the taxpayer).

The definitive appellate standard on documentation and failed research was established by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 99 DTC 5087, Docket A-710-96 (F.C.A., December 21, 1998). The taxpayer invested in developing a concrete forming medium ("spatial membrane") that produced a working prototype and a Canadian patent, but the Tax Court dismissed the appeal because the lead engineer died before trial and detailed test notebooks were missing, violating the Sass Manufacturing repeatability criterion. Reversing the Tax Court and allowing the appeal, Justice Robertson established three enduring principles: (1) failed research qualifies for SR&ED, as Regulation 2900 requires only that work be undertaken for the purpose of advancement, not that it succeed ("Presumably, not all of Alexander Graham Bell's research initiatives bore fruit"); (2) imposing an absolute documentary "repeatability criterion" where actual testing and technological advancement are proven is an error of law, as achieving a technological advance raises a prima facie inference that testing was conducted systematically; and (3) while contemporaneous documentary evidence is the "only sure-fire way" to prove systematic research, it is not legally mandatory, and credible viva voce (oral) testimony and physical prototypes are fully admissible.

Subsequent Tax Court decisions have consistently applied RIS-Christie: in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (1998), Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313 (which allowed four packaging assembly-line optimization projects, held that contemporaneous documentation is not a legal condition sine qua non under Salaison Lévesque Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 FCA 296, mandated a global assessment of the five criteria over the year, and required CRA expert witnesses to testify independently rather than relying on internal CRA policy), Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 103 (which allowed six custom frozen-pie formulation projects where failed recipes systematically eliminated options and the CEO's credible oral testimony cured documentary gaps), and 2024 TCC 159 (which allowed a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar beverage project), the Court confirmed that contemporaneous records need not be written for an uninitiated layperson and that credible oral testimony can bridge evidentiary gaps.
7.3 Technological Uncertainty, System Uncertainty, Routine Engineering, and Cost Constraints

Claims routinely fail in the Tax Court when taxpayers confuse unmeasured trial-and-error, routine engineering, or literature reviews with systematic experimental development. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, the taxpayer assembled standard motors, hydraulic pumps, and valves via trial-and-error to control theatrical fire curtain descent without employing or consulting any degreed engineers; Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed the appeal, defining a hypothesis as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" and ruling that unsystematic trial-and-error by staff lacking engineering training failed the Northwest Hydraulic test. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (aff'd 2011 FCA 355), a plastic bin manufacturer proved a systematic investigation ("How") but lost because its Statement of Agreed Facts failed to prove any technological uncertainty beyond routine thermo-forming ("Why"). In Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21, Justice Boyle dismissed an "applied research" claim for three naturopathic supplement formulations because Dr. Dahl performed only literature reviews and conceptual paper formulations without conducting any systematic empirical or laboratory testing. And in Murray Arlin Dentistry Professional Corporation v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 133, Justice Woods dismissed a periodontist's claim for 20% of his salary ($103,950/year claimed) for entering dental implant data into commercial tracking software that generated tables at the push of a button.

Conversely, the Tax Court has robustly protected claims grounded in "system uncertainty"—where combining known, off-the-shelf sub-systems creates unpredictable adverse interactions at the integrated system level that cannot be resolved by routine engineering. In 1726437 Ontario Inc. (o/a Airmax Technologies) v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376, Justice Hogan held that integrating a European boiler, an ECM fan motor, perforated flexible ductwork, and diffusers to reduce residential HVAC noise from 60 dB to 40 dB established system uncertainty and $387,553 of qualified expenditures (though the additional refundable ITC was capped at $12,000 under the Informal Procedure statute, and unpaid 2007 expenses were shifted to 2008 under subsection 127(26)). In 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77, Justice D'Auray held that system-level uncertainties (paper curling and battery drain) in an ultra-miniature wireless printer persisted in 2009–2010 even after a premature 2008 commercial release of 200 units that had to be recalled. In A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48, Justice Russell allowed SR&ED claims for building a custom 80-ton horizontal CNC lathe (system uncertainty) and an abandoned double-wheel roll grinding machine plagued by vibration, while denying claims for trying to fix third-party purchased Italian Tacchi lathes after warranty expiration.

On the boundary between cost targets and technological uncertainty, in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17, Justice Russell dismissed a claim for constructing a grid-independent, furnace-free house where the taxpayer framed its uncertainty purely around building the home "at a price point similar to a regular home," holding that "conceptually there is no technological aspect implicit in the notion of an item costing or priced at 'x' rather than 'y' dollars". Finally, in Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC 29, the Tax Court allowed four of six air-contaminant sampling projects, mapping Northwest Hydraulic Questions 1 and 4 to the "Why" and Questions 2, 3, and 5 to the "How," rejecting the CRA RTA's reliance on unverified Google searches, and confirming that "optimizing existing methods" to measure 52 airborne contaminants constituted SR&ED.
7.4 Strict Filing Deadlines, Prescribed Forms, Capital/Lease Rules, Government Assistance, and Fraud

Canadian courts strictly enforce statutory filing deadlines and assistance grinds. In 1373744 Ontario Inc. (o/a One Source Metal) v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 511, the claim was denied under subsection 37(11) where the T661 was date-stamped three days before the 18-month deadline, but the separate technical report bore no date-stamp and was faxed 12 days late. In Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301 (aff'g 2015 TCC 211), the Federal Court of Appeal held that filing Form T661 on the 18-month deadline while filing Schedule T2SCH31 six weeks late was fatal to claiming any ITC under paragraph 127(9)(m), and could not be cured by Section 32 of the Interpretation Act. In Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57 (aff'g 2017 TCC 9), the FCA held that leaving Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Form T661 violated subsection 37(11) even though the CRA had approved the same joint project for a related corporation. And in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146 (decided October 14, 2025), Justice Ouimet dismissed an application to extend the time to object where the CRA proved via automated print-to-mail affidavits that the Notices of Assessment were mailed on September 13, 2022, and the taxpayer missed the absolute 1-year-plus-90-day statutory deadline under subsection 166.2(5).

On capital and lease expenditures (newly relevant after December 15, 2024), Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen, 94 DTC 1725 (T.C.C.), established that the "all or substantially all" test for constructing an experimental prototype (a patented green-sand reclamation system) is evaluated during the SR&ED phase when the money is expended, not years later with hindsight because the prototype succeeded and continued in commercial foundry use, while Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877 (T.C.C.), established that leasing dedicated telecommunications bandwidth and remote mainframe access qualifies as an equipment lease under the Proxy Method. On government assistance, CCLC Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 96 DTC 6527 (F.C.A.), Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196, and CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57), established that repayable government contributions or low-interest loans (such as ACOA or Industry Canada SADI loans) provided on non-commercial terms that a private lender would not accept constitute "government assistance" in full under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x), reducing the SR&ED base. Finally, on litigation procedure and criminal fraud, Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58, sanctioned the Crown $25,000 in costs for breaching the implied undertaking rule by using Tax Court discovery documents to issue collateral reassessments without court leave, whereas R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora Inc., 2017 QCCQ 2684, imposed a 100% criminal fine of $1,324,294 each on the corporation and its two directors under subsection 239(1.1) for fabricating $4.5 million in subcontractor invoices to claim $1,324,294 in fraudulent SR&ED ITCs.

Meaning of "systematic investigation" & documentation
Defined systematic investigation as controlled experiments with accurate measurements; articulated early repeatability test (later tempered by FCA in RIS-Christie).

A true experimental prototype qualifies during the SR&ED phase; taxpayers are not penalized with hindsight merely because the prototype succeeded and entered commercial use.

Government assistance vs. ordinary business investment
Government funding where the province cannot earn a net commercial profit is "government assistance" under s. 12(1)(x) and s. 127(9), grinding the SR&ED base.

Section 37 must be interpreted practically to encourage Canadian industrial R&D; unprincipled audit compromise agreements bind neither the Minister nor the taxpayer.

Foundational criteria for SR&ED under s. 248(1)
Established the 5-part test (uncertainty, hypothesis, scientific method, advancement, contemporaneous records) and defined "routine engineering".

Endorsed the 5 Northwest Hydraulic questions at the appellate level; complex custom software resolved via standard practices is not SR&ED; failing to call R&D staff draws an adverse inference.

Where T661 was date-stamped before the 18-month deadline but the separate technical report lacked a stamp and was faxed late, the claim was disallowed.

TCC / FCA (2011)

Physician/dentist database tracking & time estimates
Entering clinical implant data into commercial software and preparing lectures lacked substantiation of systematic applied research hours.

System uncertainty, 180-day unpaid rule, & Informal cap

Repayable government contributions (ACOA)
Conditional/unconditional repayable government loans on non-commercial terms constitute "government assistance" that reduces the SR&ED base.

Contemporaneous documents & global project review
Contemporaneous documentation is not a legal condition sine qua non; the 5 criteria must be assessed globally over the year.

SR&ED after premature commercial product launch
System-level technological uncertainty in a miniature wireless printer continued after a failed 200-unit commercial release that had to be recalled.

Late filing of Schedule T2SCH31 (s. 127(9)(m))
Timely filing of Form T661 does not excuse filing Schedule 31 after the 18-month deadline; late filing of Schedule 31 permanently forfeits the ITC.

Trial-and-error vs. hypothesis testing & staff credentials
Unmeasured trial-and-error assembly of standard hydraulic parts by staff without engineering training or expert consultation failed the Northwest Hydraulic test.

Literature reviews without empirical testing
Desk research and conceptual supplement formulations without systematic laboratory or empirical testing do not constitute SR&ED.

Criminal fraud prosecution (s. 239(1.1))
Fabricating $4.5M in subcontractor invoices to claim $1.32M in SR&ED credits resulted in a 100% criminal fine ($1.32M each) on the company and two directors even though no refund was paid.

Blank project description boxes on Form T661
Leaving Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Form T661 violates the s. 37(11) "prescribed information" requirement and is fatal to the claim.

Custom machine tool system uncertainty vs. warranty fixes
Custom 80-ton CNC lathe and failed roll grinder qualified via system uncertainty; repairing third-party purchased Italian lathes post-warranty was denied.
6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17
Cost targets vs. technological uncertainty
Framing uncertainty purely around building a furnace-free house at a specific dollar cost ("x rather than y dollars") is a commercial objective, not a technological uncertainty.

Validity of the "scientific method" criterion
Reaffirmed that the 5 Northwest Hydraulic criteria (including the scientific method) are the binding statutory interpretation of s. 248(1).

Mapping the 5 questions to "Why" and "How"; optimization
Linked Q1 & Q4 to "Why" and Q2, Q3 & Q5 to "How"; held that optimizing analytical protocols for 52 airborne contaminants constituted SR&ED and rejected CRA's cursory Google search.

Confirmed that simplified CRA guidelines do not override Northwest Hydraulic precedent; vague software development records lacked methodical rigour.

Low-interest government R&D loans not made on strictly commercial terms are "government assistance" in full (no split between principal and interest differential).

Systematic analysis of failed frozen-pie formulations to eliminate options achieved technological advancement; credible oral testimony cured gaps in written records.

Once CRA proves mailing of Notices of Assessment via automated system affidavits, the Tax Court has no authority to extend objection deadlines beyond 1 year and 90 days.

body.text: 8. Federal Grants, Complementary Innovation Incentives, and Stacking Mechanics
8.1 National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)

Administered by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC), the Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) provides technical advisory services and non-repayable R&D contributions to incorporated, for-profit Canadian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees. According to industry advisory guides, NRC IRAP distributes roughly $414 million annually across more than 3,300 Canadian companies, reimbursing up to 80% of internal Canadian technical salaries (for T4 employees) and up to 50% of Canadian subcontractor costs across project streams ranging from $50,000 up to $10,000,000+ (with monthly claims reimbursed within 15 days).

While an NRC IRAP contribution is "government assistance" under subsection 127(18) that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 515 of Form T661, when a claimant uses the Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5 on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base (including the hours subsidized by IRAP) before the IRAP grant is deducted in Part 4. For example, as illustrated in advisory stacking analyses, if a qualifying CCPC incurs $500,000 in eligible hands-on Canadian R&D salaries under the Proxy Method, its gross federal qualified expenditure base is $500,000 (salaries) + $275,000 (55% PPA) = $775,000. Claiming federal SR&ED alone at 35% yields $271,250 (54.25% of direct salaries). If the company also receives a $100,000 NRC IRAP grant (20% of salaries), the $100,000 grant grinds the $775,000 base down to $675,000, which still generates $675,000 × 35% = $236,250 in federal SR&ED credits—for a combined recovery of $100,000 + $236,250 = $336,250, leaving the company $65,000 net ahead of claiming SR&ED alone.
8.2 Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund and Other Federal Programs

For large-scale R&D and commercialization projects, the federal Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF)—replaced by the Strategic Response Fund in 2025, to which Budget 2026 added $1 billion over six years starting in 2028–29—provides contributions covering up to 50% of technology development costs and up to 40% of commercialization costs in sectors such as AI, agri-food, biomanufacturing, and clean technology. As established in CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178, both non-repayable grants and below-market repayable SIF contributions constitute government assistance that reduces the SR&ED base. Other complementary federal programs include CanExport Innovation (covering up to 75% of international R&D partnership development costs up to $75,000), Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's AgriInnovate Program, Natural Resources Canada's Green Jobs in Natural Resources, and the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity ITCs (proposed in Budget 2026 to be extended to property available for use before 2041, alongside the proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction providing immediate 100% capital write-offs).
8.3 Comprehensive Multi-Jurisdictional Stacking Models (Worked Calculations)

To demonstrate how provincial R&D tax credits stack with the federal 35% SR&ED ITC in the 2026 taxation year (post-Bill C-15 and post-Québec CRIC), consider a stand-alone Qualifying CCPC (prior-year taxable income <$500,000; prior-year taxable capital <$15,000,000) that incurs $1,000,000 of eligible hands-on SR&ED salaries across 10 full-time non-specified employees (each earning $100,000 and spending 100% of their time on SR&ED) and elects the Proxy Method, generating a 55% PPA of $550,000 and a gross federal qualified expenditure base of $1,550,000:

items: Ontario Qualifying CCPC ($1,000,000 Salaries; $1,550,000 Gross Base Including PPA): The corporation first earns the 8% refundable OITC (Schedule 566) on the $1,550,000 base: 8% × $1,550,000 = $124,000 in cash. If the corporation is in a loss position and waives the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC to maximize immediate cash, its net federal qualified base (Line 570) is $1,550,000 − $124,000 = $1,426,000, which earns a 35% refundable federal ITC of $499,100—yielding $623,100 (62.31% of direct salaries) in immediate cash. If the corporation is profitable in Ontario and claims the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508), the ORDTC base is reduced by the $124,000 OITC to $1,426,000, generating 3.5% × $1,426,000 = $49,910 in ORDTC. Total Ontario assistance ($124,000 + $49,910 = $173,910) reduces the federal base to $1,376,090, which earns a 35% federal cash refund of $481,631.50—for a total combined tax credit recovery of $655,541.50 (65.55% of direct salaries).

Québec Qualifying CCPC ($1,000,000 Salaries in 2026): Under the Québec CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T), the $1,000,000 of Québec R&D salaries (Québec does not use a notional PPA) is reduced by the 2026 exclusion threshold (the greater of $50,000 or 10 employees × $18,952 Québec BPA = $189,520), leaving $810,480 of net qualified CRIC expenditures. At the 30% refundable CRIC rate (up to $1,000,000), the Québec cash refund is 30% × $810,480 = $243,144. Federally, the $1,550,000 gross base (salaries + 55% PPA) is reduced by the $243,144 CRIC on Line 513 to $1,306,856, earning a 35% federal cash refund of $457,399.60—for a total combined cash refund of $700,543.60 (70.05% of direct salaries).

British Columbia Qualifying CCPC or ECPC ($1,000,000 Salaries): B.C.'s 10% refundable credit (Form T666) applies to the $1,550,000 base (including PPA), yielding $155,000 in cash. The net federal base ($1,550,000 − $155,000 = $1,395,000) earns a 35% federal cash refund of $488,250—for a total combined cash refund of $643,250 (64.33% of direct salaries).

Alberta Qualifying CCPC ($1,000,000 Salaries): For an incremental R&D performer with a $0 prior two-year base, Alberta's 20% refundable IEG (AT1 Schedule 29) on the $1,550,000 base yields $310,000 in cash, and the net federal base ($1,240,000) earns a 35% federal cash refund of $434,000—for a total combined cash refund of $744,000 (74.40% of direct salaries) (or $623,100 / 62.31% for a steady-state performer earning the 8% base IEG rate).
